newsitem.title: MEXICO: Social inequality fosters illness - Americas group.
newsitem.headline: Social inequality fosters illness - Americas group.

text.p: The Panamerican Health Organisation said on Tuesday that social inequality was a major contributor in the resurgence of infectious diseases previously thought to have been wiped off the continent.

"Not only poverty in absolute terms but inequity is what most affects the community. Inequality is reflected in bad health," George Alleyne, the organisation's director general, said at a ceremony for World Health Day.

Alleyne urged regional government to design a world strategy to combat new as well as returning infectious diseases. Diseases thought to have been eradicated a century ago have been cropping up on the continent, he said.

"Tuberculosis is a new threat, AIDS continues to plague our countries and cholera, which reappeared in the Americas in 1991 after disappearing for a century, is still present," he said, adding that everyone was "vulnerable" to more resistant infectious diseases.

Mexico's Health Minister Ramon de la Fuente said about 30 percent of the world's 50 million deaths per year are from an infectious disease. "Although not all new or recurring diseases are infectious, (infectious diseases) are the most important cause of mortality in the world," he said at Tuesday's ceremony. World Health Day was officially on Monday.
He said Mexico's health system should be strengthened to combat those illnesses with a focus on lesser developed areas.
President Ernesto Zedillo echoed his words and said the government was working to iron out age-old inequality and provide equal opportunities.
